passage:
Monday. Yash met Aadhya at the campus cafe, where Aadhya's friend had introduced them. Aadhya is Deaf. Yash waved his arms and mimed drinking tea, thinking that would help, and Aadhya smiled politely but signed something quickly to the interpreter. Yash felt clumsy.

Thursday. Yash borrowed a book on Indian Sign Language, learned how to sign "hello" and "my name is", and read that the face, the space around the body and the movement all carry grammar. It is not mime. He realised his waving had been guesswork.

Next Monday. He signed "hello" and asked, using the interpreter, "Would you teach me some signs?" Aadhya's eyes lit up and both of them laughed.

qa.q: What book did Yash borrow?
qa.a: Yash borrowed a book on Indian Sign Language.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling on the first Monday, and what suggests it?
qa.a: Yash felt clumsy after his miming didn't connect, since Aadhya answered politely but turned to the interpreter. He may also have felt eager to be friendly, which is why he mimed in the first place.

qa.q: What could Yash do next to build the friendship?
qa.a: Keep learning basic signs, ask respectfully to be taught, and keep the interpreter's help until conversation grows.

qa.q: How might Aadhya have felt when Yash first mimed drinking tea?
qa.a: Aadhya probably felt polite but a little unseen, because signing is a full language and miming can seem like treating it as loose gestures.

grounding: A student learns that signed languages are complete languages using shape, movement, space and facial grammar, and respectful learning builds connection.

passage: I'm Nikita, and I'll tell you what I got wrong once, Tanuja, since you're starting at the college next month. When I was your age I shared a class with a Deaf girl called Rekha. I thought signing was just waving hands about, like charades. So I used big silly gestures at her, and I remember how patient her face was. Then her sister showed me a page on how sign language has its own grammar, faces and all, and I felt my cheeks burn. I asked Rekha to teach me a few signs, and she made me practise the alphabet till my fingers ached. We stayed friends for years. So don't guess. Ask kindly and learn the basics.

qa.q: What was the name of the Deaf girl in the elder's class?
qa.a: Her name was Rekha.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel when she saw the page about sign language?
qa.a: Nikita felt ashamed, shown by cheeks that burned, because Nikita had treated signing as charades. It could also have been a mix of shame and curiosity, since the next step was asking to learn.

qa.q: What would you advise Tanuja to do when meeting a Deaf classmate?
qa.a: Learn a few basic signs, ask kindly to be taught, and never treat signing as loose gestures or mime.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt about the big silly gestures?
qa.a: Rekha's patient face suggests she put up with it politely, though she may have felt her language was not being taken seriously.

grounding: An elder recalls learning as a student that signed languages are full languages, and that asking respectfully builds connection.

passage: The college fest stage was blasting music so loud that Akash could not hear his own voice. He had finally met Uday, the Deaf student from the photography club, and they had only ten minutes before Uday's bus. Akash tried to ask where Uday lived by miming a house and pointing, eyebrows flat, arms flapping. Uday smiled, then signed something with his eyebrows raised high and his head pushed slightly forward. His friend Nisha typed on her phone for Akash: "He's asking you a question. The eyebrows make it one." Akash stared. The raised eyebrows did the job his voice would have done. Around them, hearing people were shouting and failing, while Uday and Nisha kept signing easily across the noise. Before the bus came, Akash typed, "Can you teach me a few signs properly?" Uday nodded and signed a reply, and Nisha typed: "Saturday, library."

qa.q: How long did Akash and Uday have before Uday's bus?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when Nisha explained Uday's raised eyebrows?
qa.a: He was surprised and curious, staring as he realised the eyebrows did the work of his voice; he may also have felt a little silly about his flapping mime.

qa.q: What was a respectful step Akash took before the bus came?
qa.a: He asked Uday to teach him a few signs properly, which treated signing as a language to learn rather than something to guess at.

qa.q: What might it be like for Uday when Akash mimes with flapping arms?
qa.a: Uday smiles, so he may find it friendly but also a sign that Akash sees signing as acting out, not a language with its own grammar.

grounding: Shows a student discovering that facial grammar and structure make sign language a full language, not mime, in a noisy setting.

passage: Wasim was the only hearing person at Tanvir's birthday dinner in a Pune café. Tanvir's Deaf friends signed fast across the table, laughing, and Wasim tried to join in by waving his hands and pulling faces, the way he might play charades. Tanvir's sister Farah watched him, amused but tired. Then Wasim noticed something. When Farah told a story about two friends, she set one to her left and one to her right in the air, and later just pointed back to those spots instead of repeating them. Her face changed with every line. It was like watching someone keep a map as they spoke. Wasim put his hands down. He typed on his phone and turned it to Tanvir: "I've been acting things out. That's not how it works, is it? Can you show me how to say happy birthday properly?" Tanvir grinned and taught him.

qa.q: Where was Tanvir's birthday dinner?
qa.a: In a Pune café.

qa.q: Why did Wasim put his hands down during Farah's story?
qa.a: He seemed to feel embarrassed and newly respectful once he saw she was using space and her face like a grammar; he may also have been simply fascinated.

qa.q: What small step helped Wasim connect with Tanvir?
qa.a: He admitted he had been acting things out and asked Tanvir to show him how to sign happy birthday properly.

qa.q: How might Farah see Wasim's charades-style waving?
qa.a: She watched it amused but tired, which suggests she has seen hearing people treat signing as loose gestures many times.

grounding: Shows a hearing young adult realising sign language uses space and facial grammar as a full language and asking to learn.

passage:
"Okay, so sign language is basically miming, right?" Nilesh asked as they queued for coffee.
Maria put down her cup. "Where did that come from?"
"Your cousin Joel at the party. I tried acting out 'Do you want food?' and he looked at me like I was a toddler."
Maria laughed. "Joel's Deaf, not bored. He's got a whole language. Handshape, movement, where the sign is made, his face. Change one and it's a different word."
"Even the face?"
"Especially the face. His eyebrows can turn a sentence into a question."
Nilesh groaned. "So I was doing baby charades at him."
"A bit." Maria softened. "He'd rather you try. Just try properly. Ask him to teach you the greeting, and learn the alphabet to spell your name."
"Would he mind me asking?"
"He'd mind you guessing more."

qa.q: Where did Nilesh meet Maria's cousin Joel?
qa.a: At the party.

qa.q: How does Nilesh feel when he realises what his miming looked like?
qa.a: He groans, which suggests he feels embarrassed about doing "baby charades"; he also seems eager, asking whether Joel would mind being asked.

qa.q: What would you advise Nilesh before he meets Joel again?
qa.a: Follow Maria's advice: ask Joel to teach him the greeting and learn the alphabet to spell his name, instead of guessing with mime.

qa.q: How might Joel have felt when Nilesh acted out food?
qa.a: He may have felt talked down to, like being treated as a toddler, since Nilesh treated his language as loose miming.

grounding: Shows a student learning from a friend that a sign language is a complete language with its own grammar and that asking respectfully builds connection.

passage: I'm Ramesh, and for my first month in the engineering hostel I thought I understood Vasudha's signing because I'm good at charades. When she signed to her friends in the canteen, I'd guess along: that must be food, that must be tired. I even tried joining in with made-up gestures. One day she wrote in my notebook: "It's not mime. It's Indian Sign Language. It has grammar." Then she showed me. The same hand movement changed when her eyebrows went up, turning it into a question. Where she placed people in the space in front of her mattered too; later she could point back to that spot instead of repeating a name. My ears went hot. I had treated her language like a party game. Now I'm in a Saturday class, fumbling through handshapes, and I ask Vasudha when I'm unsure. Sometimes she laughs at my attempts, and I've learnt to laugh too.

qa.q: What did Vasudha write in Ramesh's notebook?
qa.a: "It's not mime. It's Indian Sign Language. It has grammar."

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel after Vasudha showed how her signing worked?
qa.a: Ramesh felt embarrassed, ears going hot, on seeing that guessing along and made-up gestures had treated her language like a party game.

qa.q: What is Ramesh doing now that builds the friendship?
qa.a: Taking a Saturday class and asking Vasudha respectfully when unsure, instead of guessing.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Vasudha when Ramesh joined in with made-up gestures?
qa.a: She may have felt her language was being treated as a game rather than respected, which is why she explained that it has grammar.

grounding: It illustrates a student learning that a Deaf friend's signing is a full language with facial grammar and use of space, not mime, and choosing to learn and ask respectfully.
